title: Building the Ephemeral Collab Editor: OT vs CRDT, and other rabbit holes
content:
This is so complicated oh my GOD.... (On the other hand of my shameless complaining, I'm actually being challenged, yay...!)

I set out to build a Google-Docs-style collaborative code editor — ephemeral, real-time, multiple cursors. Here's what I ran into.

## Keeping the WebSocket traffic sane

Sending web traffic for websockets can get quite convoluted, so I scoped it down: I'm only syncing cursor movement + text changes. And I do not want to pay for storage — everything in the free tier is good enough for a project. Paying for S3 (or Azure, w/e) cloud storage would be wild.

There's a ton of ways to save on server-client communication, for example:

- **What if a user goes to absolute town on the keyboard?** Multiply those karens by 10 and our servers can't keep up (think of 10 keyboard andy's...). ALRIGHTY, you force my hand — I MUST, and I MEAN MUST, not have the server be overloaded by this shenanigans. I throttle up to ~300ms once the user is done executing their fierce keyboard-warrior text.
- **What about cursor boys who love to spam clicks?** We can debounce those to ~50ms packet sends and the user won't know the diff. (Hey, could we scale that to 250ms? PMs & Data Analysts, GET ON IT — let's have a fierce debate on whatever number you think is correct, LOL.)

## The mid-session join problem

What if a user joins mid-session? We need to display the *current state* of the document. My first answer: there are probably compression techniques to make this incredibly efficient, but I'll just send the entire file over — don't blame me for not going into a deep dive.

...Never mind. Apparently I'm going deep on this. There's an incredibly confusing but INTERESTING concept here: **OT (Operational Transformation) vs CRDT (Conflict-free Replicated Data Types)**.

- **Operational Transformation** is like a master/slave approach — the server is authoritative and decides who writes where. Say User A writes "X" to index 0 and User B writes "Y" to index 0 simultaneously: the server says "UMMM ACTUALLY User B, you are WRONG, go to index 1 instead lmao."
- **CRDTs** are the "mathematical approach." Not server-authoritative — instead, every character gets a unique ID based on its position relative to other characters. When User A inserts "X" and User B inserts "Y" at the same index, the result is mathematically guaranteed to converge to the same document on every screen.

If you're curious, here are the resources that broke my brain: [Yjs](https://github.com/yjs/yjs) and [Figma's engineering blog on multiplayer](https://www.figma.com/blog/how-figmas-multiplayer-technology-works/). Hello Interview recently did a video about this real time collaboration editor, here's a [link](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=EX5uZV3Tzss) and these staff level engineers do a great job explaining it in further detail, check it out!

Taking a step back, some of these designs are so well structured and despite my best efforts this is rather difficult. I think I learned quite a lot about this and it's safe to say that I really admire these engineers and hope to be like them some day!

## How it ended

Rabbit hole aside — I ended up using an open-source library that bundles all of this up quite nicely: **Yjs**. God send. Which means all of my work anticipating the websocket connection handling was kinda wasted... remarkable... so... BRUH.

The last piece was auth: confirming connections with my backend to verify SSO tokens, because I wouldn't want some random person tinkering with my "ephemeral docs" kekw. The flow ended up as: Google sign-in → backend verifies the Firebase token and signs a site JWT → the JWT gets exchanged for a single-use, 30-second WebSocket ticket → the socket upgrades only with a valid ticket. Try it on the [Collaborate page](https://eddiewwu.vercel.app/collaborate).
